job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — Per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000-ton threshold applies to a “single vessel,” so an operator could split recovery among several vessels and keep each below the threshold. The text does not say whether tonnage is measured per calendar year, fiscal year, or another period, or how partial years and transferred or stockpiled material count.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Narrow or uncertain activity covered.** “Recovery” may not reach exploration, seabed disturbance without collection, or other preparatory work, and “polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources” does not specify what resources or recovery methods qualify. The 200-meter depth cutoff may also leave shallower seabed extraction outside the definition.

3. **Section 2(1)(B) — Discretionary risk test.** The Secretary may bring other activities within the definition, but the bill gives no criteria, process, deadline, or guidance for deciding what risks are “comparable.” Until the Secretary acts, operators could argue that an unlisted activity is not covered.

4. **Section 2(2) and Section 3(a) — Limited definition of U.S. person.** “U.S. person” covers citizens and corporations organized under state law, but not expressly U.S. residents, partnerships, LLCs, trusts, or other entities. It also does not cover a foreign subsidiary merely because it is owned or controlled by a U.S. corporation.

5. **Section 2(3) and Section 4(a) — Vessel-registration gap.** Registration applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons that are “equipped” for recovery, leaving smaller vessels and vessels whose equipment status is disputed outside the registry. “Equipped” is undefined, and the bill does not say how an operator can register a vessel that does not qualify as “covered.”

6. **Section 3(a) — Unclear reach and covered conduct.** “Any person in the United States” could mean a person physically present here, a person acting here, or a person otherwise subject to U.S. jurisdiction; “engage in” is also undefined. The text does not expressly address financing, contracting, transporting, processing, purchasing, or facilitating mining, leaving room to argue that those activities are not prohibited.

7. **Section 3(b) — Broad existing-operations exception.** The exception has no end date and does not limit mining to exploration, require a transition plan, or specify who may rely on the pre-enactment license. Operators could argue that substantial commercial mining remains protected so long as it is conducted “under” an earlier exploration license.

8. **Section 3(c) — Unbounded assessment exception.** The bill sets no standards, limits, approval process, or reporting requirements for activities said to be “for the purpose of environmental assessment.” An operator could characterize extraction or other otherwise prohibited activity as assessment work.

9. **Section 4 — Reporting without an effective compliance framework.** The bill sets no registration deadline or report format, verification method, audit authority, or consequence for failing to register or report; it also requires reports only from registered operators. Reports describe recovery activities, not necessarily where, when, or how much was recovered, and the text does not expressly require a report when no recovery occurred.

10. **Section 5(a) — Civil-penalty uncertainty.** “Not more than” $1 million leaves the penalty amount and assessment process unspecified, and “for each day” does not clarify how continuing violations, multiple vessels, or separate acts are counted. The section also does not identify who assesses or collects the penalty or provide an express enforcement procedure.

11. **Section 5(b) — Criminal-enforcement gaps.** The bill does not define “willfully,” which can invite disputes over the mental state required for conviction. It also does not specify who investigates or prosecutes, or expressly provide for forfeiture, vessel detention, or other measures that could stop ongoing operations.

12. **Section 6 — International agreement is not guaranteed.** The Secretary need only “seek to negotiate” an agreement; the bill does not require an agreement to be reached, set out what happens if negotiations fail, or make the prohibition depend on other countries adopting equivalent rules.

13. **Section 7(a) — Unclear lifting standard and process.** “Without serious harm” is undefined, and the bill sets no deadline or required contents for the National Academies’ report. The text also does not explain what happens if the report is delayed or inconclusive; a joint resolution would still have to complete the ordinary enactment process to change the law.

14. **Section 7(b) — Conflict with the continuing prohibition.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes a specified finding, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless of that finding. The sunset could therefore terminate the prohibition without the report or congressional finding contemplated in subsection (a).
